To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the majority of Copperbelt residents are aware of how to prevent HIV/AIDS; (2) the majority of the population has not adopted safe behaviors; (3) the majority of respondents believe that HIV/AIDS is preventable; (4) the majority of residents have not adopted safe behaviors because they are not able to do so; and (5) the majority of those who are able to adopt safe behaviors are men, and the majority of those not able to adopt safe behavior are women
social and economic factors play a significant role in limiting behavior change, and that gender imbalances are a particularly large obstacle to behavior change.

(1) HIV/AIDS prevention programs based on IEC alone have not been effective at modifying behavior in the Copperbelt; (2) social factors, particularly gender inequality, are the primary obstacles to behavior change, with economic factors playing only a secondary role; and (3) HIV/AIDS interventions in the Copperbelt need to be expanded to include gender-specific community development programs that target men.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV prevention efforts in Zambia, and probably in many other developing countries as well, are unlikely to succeed until the underlying social and economic problems of the region are addressed.
HIV prevention in Africa is not a problem of lack of knowledge, but rather of the lack of social and economic empowerment of the people.
the social and economic factors that operate as fundamental obstacles for behavior change are not just a few, but many, and they operate in a complex way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HIV epidemic in Zambia is a result of a complex interaction of social and economic factors and the HIV epidemic will not be controlled without addressing these factors.
while HIV interventions have been successful in raising awareness of AIDS and how to prevent its transmission, the interventions have not succeeded in changing behavior.
HIV interventions must be designed to address the social and economic factors that are the root causes of the problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV interventions need a broader approach that goes beyond the individual and addresses the social, economic, and cultural context in which individuals live.
HIV interventions must address the social and economic factors that are fundamental obstacles to behavior modification.
HIV interventions must be more comprehensive and address a wider range of issues in order to be successful in Africa.
